0.title: Mirror, Fence and Guide
0.essay:
Few words make modern people bristle like the word “law”. Yet the longest chapter in the Bible is a love song about God’s law: “Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day” (Psalm 119:97). How can anyone love a law? And what is a Christian, saved by grace, meant to do with it?

Two half-truths

Many believers carry two sayings of Scripture without knowing how they fit. Paul says, “you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:14). Jesus says, “I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). Hold only the first and the law looks like an old enemy we have escaped. Hold only the second and grace begins to look like a fresh start on the same treadmill. Paul himself asked the question this study asks: “Why then the law?” (Galatians 3:19).

An old and careful answer

The Reformers gave a careful answer. God’s moral law, they said, has three uses. It is a mirror that shows us our sin and sends us to Christ. It is a fence that restrains evil in a fallen world. And it is a guide that shows those already saved how to walk in love. John Calvin set this out in his Institutes of the Christian Religion (book 2, chapter 7), and it is the teaching of the great Reformed confessions, including the 1689 Baptist Confession this commentary follows.

Lutherans also teach three uses, and their Formula of Concord (1577) gave the third its own article. But they usually number them differently, putting the restraining use first and the mirror second (as the study The Ten Commandments also does). This study follows Calvin’s order, as this commentary’s Positions do. The order differs; the substance is the same.

Where this study fits

The Ten Commandments walks through each commandment. Reading the Old Testament Well asks what to do with Israel’s other laws, and Hermeneutics with reading the Bible as a whole. Good Works looks at the life the law describes. This study asks a simpler and deeper question: what does God do with his law in a human life?

The answer will take us, again and again, to one place. The law is not a ladder up to God. In his hands it shows us our need, guards the weak, lights the path, and at every turn it points to the only person who ever kept it, and who kept it for us.

The chapters

What Is the Law?; The First Use: A Mirror; The Second Use: A Fence; The Third Use: A Guide; Law and Gospel; and Christ and the Law.

For reflection

When you hear the word “law”, what do you feel: fear, boredom, guilt, gratitude? Which of the two sayings, “not under law” or “not to abolish but to fulfill”, have you leaned on more, and why?

1.title: What Is the Law?
1.essay:
Ask most people what “the law” is and they picture a courtroom, a parking ticket or a speed camera. Ask an Israelite and you would get a different picture: a father sitting with his child at the end of the day, teaching him how to live.

Instruction from a Father

The Hebrew word usually translated “law” is torah. Its basic meaning is teaching or instruction, and it comes from a root that has to do with pointing the way. It is the word a parent uses in Proverbs: “Hear, my son, your father’s instruction, and forsake not your mother’s teaching” (Proverbs 1:8). The word for “teaching” there is torah. When Israel heard “the law of the LORD”, they did not first think of a penal code. They thought of the LORD showing his people the way, and so the psalmist can sing, “The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul” (Psalm 19:7).

The Bible uses the word “law” in several ways, and it helps to notice which one is meant. It can mean the Ten Commandments; the whole covenant God made with Israel at Sinai, with its priests, sacrifices and civil rules; the first five books of the Bible, which Jesus called “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44); or God’s moral will in general. When Paul says Christians are “not under law”, he is usually speaking of the Sinai covenant as a whole, as a way of standing before God. When he says “the law is holy”, he is speaking of what God commands. Much confusion clears when we ask, “Which law?”

Rescue first

The order in which God gave the law matters enormously. Before a single command at Sinai, God said, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). He had already said, “I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself” (Exodus 19:4). Israel did not keep the law in order to be rescued. They were rescued, and then they were given the law. The study The Ten Commandments draws this out at length.

So the law was a gift, and Israel was meant to see it as one. Moses told them that the nations would hear these statutes and say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people” (Deuteronomy 4:6). God commanded them “for our good always” (Deuteronomy 6:24).

Older than Sinai

But the moral law did not begin at Sinai. Paul says that even those who never had the written law “show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness” (Romans 2:15). The 1689 Confession begins its chapter on the law in the garden of Eden. God made human beings in his image, and his will for them was built into them from the start. At Sinai he wrote it down, in stone, “with the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18), so that a forgetful people could not miss it.

That is why the moral law is not arbitrary. It is God’s own character translated into human life. He is faithful, so we must not commit adultery. He is truth, so we must not lie. He gives, so we must not steal. “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16). Jesus summed it all up in two commands, love for God and love for neighbour, and said, “On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:40).

Three strands

Christians have long found it helpful to sort the laws of Moses into three kinds. The ceremonial laws (sacrifices, priesthood, festivals, food laws) were pictures of Christ, “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17). The civil laws governed Israel as a nation in its land. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, expresses God’s unchanging will for all people. With the 1689 Confession, this commentary holds that the civil and ceremonial laws are fulfilled and ended, while the moral law remains the rule of life, as the shape of love and never as a way to earn salvation.

This division is a helpful map, not a set of sealed boxes; the study Reading the Old Testament Well, in its chapter “The Law and the Christian”, weighs its strengths and limits. When this study speaks of the three uses of the law, it means the moral law.

The law of Christ

Christians are not lawless. Paul says he is “not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21). He tells the Galatians, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). The law of Christ is not a new, softer law that replaces the old one. It is the same holy will of God, taught by Jesus, filled out by his example (“just as I have loved you”, John 13:34), and written on the heart by his Spirit.

A woman grew up in a home where rules were enforced by a cold and angry father. The word “law” still makes her shoulders tense. Reading Exodus 20 slowly with an older friend, she notices that God speaks his name and his rescue before a single command. “He carries them out first,” she says quietly, “and then he tells them how to live as free people.” She begins to hear the commandments in a different voice: not a jailer’s, but a Father’s.

That is the voice of the law as God meant it. The same God who wrote with his finger on stone would one day write on hearts. And the same God who said “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out” (Exodus 20:2) would one day bring his people out of a deeper slavery, at the cost of his own Son.

For reflection

Does it change how you feel about God’s law to know that torah means instruction, the word a father uses? Why does it matter that the rescue came before the commands? Which “law” do you think Paul means in Romans 6:14, and why does the question matter? Where have you heard God’s commands in a jailer’s voice rather than a Father’s?

2.title: The First Use: A Mirror
2.essay:
A mirror cannot wash your face. It can only show you that your face needs washing. Calvin compared the first use of the law to a mirror: in it we see our weakness, then our sin, and then the curse that sin deserves. It is an uncomfortable thing to look into. It is also one of God’s great mercies.

The knowledge of sin

Paul puts it plainly. “For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20). The law speaks “so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God” (Romans 3:19). Before the law, we argue, excuse and compare. When it speaks, our mouths close.

Paul knew this from the inside. Before he met Christ he could describe himself, “as to righteousness under the law, blameless” (Philippians 3:6). His outward life was in order. Then one commandment reached him: “I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Romans 7:7). The tenth commandment does not ask about actions at all. It asks about desire. A man can keep his hands clean; he cannot keep his heart clean by trying. The mirror showed Paul what his good record had hidden.

Jesus does the same in the Sermon on the Mount, tracing murder back to anger and adultery back to the look of the eye (Matthew 5:21–28). The law, read as Jesus reads it, leaves no one standing. “None is righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10).

Why the law can make things worse

There is something stranger still. Paul says that sin, “seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness” (Romans 7:8). Put up a sign saying “Keep off the grass” and something in us wants to walk on it. Augustine remembered stealing pears as a teenager, not because he was hungry (he threw most of them to the pigs), but because it was forbidden. The law does not create our sin, but it provokes it and exposes it.

Is the law to blame, then? No. It is “holy and righteous and good” (Romans 7:12). The fault is in us. God’s purpose was “that sin might be shown to be sin” (Romans 7:13). Sin that is hidden can never be healed. “Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

The law cannot save

Paul asks whether the law is against God’s promises. “Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law” (Galatians 3:21). No such law exists. The law can tell us what love looks like, but it cannot give us a heart that loves. And it pronounces a sentence: “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them” (Galatians 3:10).

That sounds hopeless. It is meant to sound hopeless, but only for a moment. “The Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe” (Galatians 3:22). The prison has a door, and the door has a name.

A guardian who walks us to Christ

“So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith” (Galatians 3:24). The guardian in a Greek or Roman household was a trusted slave who walked a child to school, kept him out of trouble and disciplined him. His job was to deliver the child to the teacher. Paul is speaking of the Sinai covenant’s place in history, holding Israel until Christ came, but the same pattern is repeated in many lives. The law takes us by the hand, often roughly, and walks us to Christ.

John Bunyan pictured it in The Pilgrim’s Progress. In the Interpreter’s house, Christian is shown a parlour thick with dust. A man starts to sweep, and the dust flies up until everyone is choking. Then a girl sprinkles the room with water, and it is swept clean with ease. The dust, the Interpreter explains, is the sin of the heart; the sweeper is the law; the water is the gospel. The law stirs our sin up and shows it to us. Only the gospel cleans the room.

How it feels, and why it is mercy

When young King Josiah heard the book of the law read, “he tore his clothes” (2 Kings 22:11). When Ezra read it, “all the people wept as they heard the words of the Law” (Nehemiah 8:9). The mirror hurts.

But a doctor who shows you the scan is not being cruel. He is showing you why you need the operation. The tax collector in Jesus’ parable had seen himself in the mirror. He “would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’” (Luke 18:13). And Jesus said that he “went down to his house justified” (Luke 18:14). The Pharisee beside him had never truly looked.

A businessman thought of himself as decent: faithful, generous, honest. Then he heard a sermon on Matthew 5:22 and thought of the brother he had not spoken to in eleven years, and the contempt he still nursed. He could not sleep that night. For the first time in his life he prayed like the tax collector. Years later he says that sermon was the worst night of his life and the beginning of the best thing in it.

The mirror and the believer

The first use does not end at conversion. Believers still see their sin in the law, and it sends them back to Christ day by day.

But the mirror is for looking into and then looking away, to Christ. Some tender believers keep staring, and every glance becomes fresh condemnation. If that is you, hear this: the law’s work is to send you to Christ, not to keep you from him. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). The study Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation speaks to this at length. If guilt has become constant and tormenting, speak to your pastor or a biblical counsellor, who may also ask you to see your doctor; asking for help is no failure of faith.

For reflection

Which commandment has acted most like a mirror for you? Why does the law sometimes stir up the very sin it forbids? How is it mercy that the law cannot save us? When you see your sin, do you tend to look away to Christ, or keep staring?

3.title: The Second Use: A Fence
3.essay:
A fence at the top of a cliff does not change the heart of the child who runs towards the edge. It does not make her wise, or obedient, or grateful. It simply keeps her alive. That is the second use of the law.

A fence for a fallen world

Calvin described the second use like this: there are people who care nothing for what is right unless they are forced to, but when they hear the law’s threats, fear of punishment holds them back from at least some of the evil they would otherwise do. Their hearts are not changed. Their hands are restrained. This is not salvation, and it is not holiness. But it is a great kindness to everyone who lives near them.

Imagine a single week in your town with no laws at all, no courts, no police and no consequences. Most of us would lock the door and keep the children in. The fact that we can walk to the shops, send our children to school and sleep at night is, in part, the law doing its second work.

The law is for the lawless

Paul writes, “Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully, understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners” (1 Timothy 1:8–9). Then he gives a list: those who strike their parents, murderers, the sexually immoral, enslavers, liars and perjurers. Read it slowly and you will notice that it runs through the second half of the Ten Commandments, from honouring parents to bearing false witness. “Enslavers” are kidnappers and traders in human beings, the worst kind of theft.

The law names evil, sets a boundary and threatens a penalty for people who will not do right of their own accord. Someone who loves his neighbour does not need a law to stop him murdering her. But the world is not full of such people, and neither is any human heart.

God’s servant for your good

God has given government to carry this fence into public life. “For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad” (Romans 13:3). The ruler “is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4). Peter says the same: governors are sent “to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good” (1 Peter 2:14).

Civil laws are not the same as God’s law, but the best of them reflect it. Laws against murder, theft, fraud and perjury rest on what God wrote on human hearts. And Israel’s own laws show God’s concern for the common good: honest weights in the market (Deuteronomy 25:13–15), courts that refuse bribes (“Justice, and only justice, you shall follow”, Deuteronomy 16:20), and harvest edges left “for the poor and for the sojourner” (Leviticus 19:10). Israel’s civil laws have ended with the nation they governed, but the justice they express still teaches.

So Christians can value good laws and work for them as one way of loving their neighbours. William Wilberforce and his friends spent twenty years persuading Parliament to end the British slave trade, which it did in 1807. Martin Luther King Jr. used to point out that a law could not make a man love him, but it could keep a man from lynching him, and that this mattered a great deal. Both men understood the second use of the law, whether or not they called it that. One caution: the church preaches God’s whole moral law, with its public consequences, but its pulpit is not a platform for parties, and on many policy questions faithful Christians will disagree.

What a fence cannot do

The second use has real limits, and it is honest to name them.

A fence cannot change a heart. The law, Paul says, was “weakened by the flesh” (Romans 8:3). It can stop a thief stealing from you; it cannot make him generous. Societies that try to make people good simply by passing laws are always disappointed.

Legal is not the same as righteous. Jesus said that Moses permitted divorce “because of your hardness of heart” (Mark 10:5). Civil law sometimes has to settle for less than God’s full will, because it governs hard hearts. So “it’s legal” never settles whether something is right, and a nation’s laws are not the measure of a Christian’s conscience.

The fence is not the gospel. A well-ordered society is a gift, but it does not save anyone. A respectable person, kept from scandal by fear of disgrace, may be as far from God as anyone in prison. The second use keeps the world from tearing itself apart while the gospel goes out. It holds back the flood; it does not bring the harvest.

Theonomists, wanting to honour all of Scripture, hold that Israel’s civil laws and penalties should guide modern governments. This commentary holds that those laws were given to one nation in one land and expired with it, though their justice still instructs (see Reading the Old Testament Well). The study Common Grace explores more fully how God holds back evil in a fallen world, and The Christian & the World looks at government.

The fence and the people God will save

Calvin noticed something beautiful here. Many people whom God will later save are kept by this fence long before they know him. Fear of the law, of shame or of consequences holds them back from sins that would have wrecked their lives, until the day grace reaches them.

A woman who came to faith in her thirties looks back on her teenage years. She was reckless and angry, but the thought of losing her driving licence kept her from driving drunk, and a strict headteacher kept her in school. She did not love God then. She was not even trying to be good. But she now sees a hand on her shoulder that she did not notice at the time. “I thought I was getting away with things,” she says. “I was being kept.”

That is what the second use of the law is: God’s patient hand on a runaway world. He does not let it fall all the way, because he has not finished saving it. “God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance” (Romans 2:4).

For reflection

What would your street look like for one week with no laws at all? Why does Paul say the law is not laid down for the just? Can you think of something legal in your society that is still wrong, and how should a Christian live with that? Where can you see the law’s restraint in your own life before you knew Christ, or since?

4.title: The Third Use: A Guide
4.essay:
“Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). A lamp is not a burden to a traveller walking at night. It is the thing that lets him walk without falling. Calvin called this the principal use of the law, the one closest to its true purpose: it is for believers, in whose hearts the Spirit of God already lives and reigns.

A delight, not a dread

The first psalm describes the blessed person: “his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2). And Psalm 119, all 176 verses of it, is a love song to God’s word: “Oh how I love your law!” (Psalm 119:97).

These were redeemed people, not people earning salvation, and they had found in God’s law the shape of a good life: “I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!” (Psalm 119:32). “I shall walk in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts” (Psalm 119:45). The law, for them, was not a cage but open country. A fish is not imprisoned by water, a train is not enslaved by its rails, and a vine is not crushed by the trellis that holds it up to the sun. They flourish in them, and only in them.

Love has a shape

When Paul gives Christians the law as a guide, he gives it as the shape of love. “Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law” (Romans 13:8). The commandments against adultery, murder, theft and coveting “are summed up in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law” (Romans 13:9–10).

This guards against two mistakes. Love without law becomes vague and sentimental; it can justify almost anything, including adultery “because we love each other”. Law without love becomes cold and proud, like the Pharisees who tithed their garden herbs and “neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (Matthew 23:23). The commandments tell love what it looks like on an ordinary Tuesday: in the marriage bed, the tax return, the conversation about a colleague behind her back.

And Jesus ties it to himself. “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15). John adds, “his commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3). Not because they are easy, but because they are his, and he has made us his.

Written on the heart

Here is the wonder of the new covenant. At Sinai, God sighed over his people: “Oh that they had such a heart as this always, to fear me and to keep all my commandments” (Deuteronomy 5:29). Centuries later he answered his own longing with a promise: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). And through Ezekiel: “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27).

Notice what is new. Not a new law, but a new heart. The same holy will that was carved on stone is now written “not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3). Augustine prayed that God would give what he commands, and then command whatever he wills. In the new covenant God does exactly that.

A lamp, and sometimes a spur

Calvin added that believers need the law in two ways. As a lamp, it teaches us more clearly every day what God’s will is. As a spur, it rouses us, because even renewed hearts are often sluggish. He compared the flesh to a lazy donkey that will not move without the whip. Anyone who has known the Christian life for long will recognise the picture.

Where Christians differ

Antinomianism (from Greek words meaning “against law”) takes several forms. In the 1530s Johann Agricola, once one of Luther’s own students, argued in effect that the law belonged in the courts and not in the pulpit, and that repentance should be preached from the gospel alone; Luther wrote firmly against him. Others since have taught that believers are led directly by the Spirit and need no commands. At full strength, their concern is serious: Paul does say “you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:14) and “if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law” (Galatians 5:18), and they fear that commands, however well meant, will slowly turn grace back into a treadmill.

Lutheran caution. Lutherans affirm a third use (the Formula of Concord gives it a whole article), but they stress, with Melanchthon, that the law always accuses. Because believers are still sinners, even the law’s guidance stings the old nature, and it never gives the power to obey. Some modern Lutheran theologians have doubted the third use altogether. Their great concern is that the gospel must never be swallowed up by moralism, and that the Christian must always live from Christ, not from his own progress.

New Covenant Theology holds that the whole covenant of Sinai, the Ten Commandments included, has ended as a covenant, and that Christians are under the law of Christ, which takes up the moral commands the New Testament repeats.

This commentary’s view: with the 1689 Confession, believers are not under the law as a covenant of works, to be justified or condemned by it; Christ has dealt with that once for all. But the moral law remains the rule of life for believers, as the shape of love and never as a way to earn salvation. “Not under law” means not under its curse or under it as the way to stand before God; it does not mean without God’s will, for Paul is “under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21). The Lutheran caution is wise and should be heard: the law guides but never empowers; only the Spirit gives life; and because we are still sinners, the third use never leaves the first behind. Every time the law guides us, it also shows us how far we fall short, and sends us back to Christ. On one point this commentary differs from the Confession, holding the Sabbath command fulfilled in Christ; the study Worship & the Lord’s Day explains why, and honours those who see it otherwise.

The law in an ordinary week

A young woman is applying for a job she badly wants. A friend suggests she exaggerate her experience; everyone does it. She thinks of the ninth commandment, and it comes to her not as a threat but as her Father’s voice, telling her what love and truth look like here. She writes the honest version. She does not get the job. But she sleeps well, with nothing to hide. The law did not save her. It showed her how a saved person walks.

For reflection

Which picture of the law helps you most: a lamp, a trellis, rails for a train, or open country? Why is it dangerous to have love without law, or law without love? What is new about the new covenant, if not a new law? Which of the views in “Where Christians differ” do you find most attractive, and what would it be in danger of losing?

5.title: Law and Gospel
5.essay:
Martin Luther once said, in effect, that anyone who knows how to tell the law and the gospel apart should thank God and know that he is a real theologian. He did not mean that it is a trick for experts. He meant that almost every spiritual sickness comes from mixing them up, and almost every healing begins when they are put back in their places.

Two words from one God

The law and the gospel both come from God, and both are good. But they say different things. The law says, “Do this and live.” Paul quotes it: “The one who does them shall live by them” (Galatians 3:12). The gospel says, “It is done; believe and live.” The law tells us what we must do for God. The gospel tells us what God has done for us. The law demands; the gospel gives. “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

That does not make the law the villain. “Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law” (Romans 3:31). The law tells us why we need the gospel and, once we have it, how to live it.

Kept apart: how we are saved

On the question of how a sinner is made right with God, law and gospel must never be mixed. “A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ” (Galatians 2:16). Paul’s letter to the Galatians is a cry of alarm on exactly this point. Teachers had arrived in the churches of Galatia saying that faith in Christ was good, but that Gentile believers must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be fully accepted. Paul answered, “if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (Galatians 2:21). Add one condition to Christ, however small, and you have a different gospel, which is no gospel at all.

The same mixing happens today in quieter forms. It sounds like this: “God accepts you if you believe sincerely enough.” “You were saved by grace, but you stay saved by trying hard.” “God will love you more after a good week.” Each time, the good news has become a new demand, and the weary are handed one more weight.

Held together: how we live

But law and gospel are not only distinct. They are joined. Augustine put it memorably: the law was given so that grace would be sought, and grace was given so that the law would be fulfilled. The law sends us to Christ; Christ sends us back to the law, not as a ladder to climb but as a path to walk with him.

Paul says it in one sentence: “For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Romans 8:3–4). The law could not save. The Son did. And the result is that the law’s righteous requirement is fulfilled in us, by the Spirit.

The Heidelberg Catechism is built on this pattern. It has three parts: our misery, our deliverance and our gratitude. The law appears near the beginning, where it asks how we know our misery and answers, from the law of God. And the Ten Commandments appear again near the end, in the part on gratitude, as the shape of a thankful life. The same law, first as a mirror and then as a guide, with the gospel standing between them.

Twin errors

Get this wrong and you fall into one of two ditches. Legalism treats the law as the way to win or keep God’s favour. Licence treats grace as permission to ignore the law. They look like opposites. Timothy Keller often pointed out that there are two ways to try to be your own saviour and lord: by breaking all the rules, or by keeping them all. The younger son in Jesus’ parable ran from his father; the elder brother stayed home and served him like a hired hand. Neither trusted the father’s love.

Sinclair Ferguson has argued that legalism and licence are not opposites at all but twins, born of the same lie: the serpent’s whisper in Eden that God is holding out on us. The legalist thinks God’s favour must be earned; the licentious thinks God’s commands must be escaped. Both have misjudged the heart of God. The cure for both is the same: not a little more law for the one and a little more grace for the other, but a fresh sight of the God who gives his Son freely and whose every command is love. The study The Grace of God explores the two errors further.

A man grew up in a church where nearly every sermon ended with, “Do more. Pray more. Witness more.” By forty he was exhausted and quietly resentful of God. Then he read Galatians straight through in one sitting. He wept at “the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). Over the next year something surprised him. He found himself praying more, not less, and wanting to obey for the first time in years. The demands had not changed. The voice behind them had.

Preaching both

So faithful preaching needs both words, each in its place. The proud and comfortable need the law to strip away their excuses. The broken and guilty need the gospel to lift their heads. And the forgiven need the law again, as their Father’s guidance, heard in the warmth of the gospel. Only law produces Pharisees or despair; only comfort leaves people unsure what they were saved from, and what they were saved for.

In eighteenth-century Scotland the Marrow controversy turned on this question. Some ministers taught that sinners must first forsake their sins before they were warranted to come to Christ. Thomas Boston and his friends answered that Christ is offered freely to sinners as they are, and that true holiness grows from receiving him, not from qualifying for him. The New Testament stands with them. We do not clean ourselves up in order to come to the gospel. We come, and the gospel begins to clean us up.

That order is the whole difference between a slave and a son. The slave obeys in order to be accepted. The son obeys because he already is.

For reflection

Can you put the difference between law and gospel into a sentence of your own? In what quiet ways do you turn the gospel back into law? Which ditch do you drift towards, legalism or licence, and what lie about God lies beneath it? How does Augustine’s summary, law given so that grace would be sought, grace given so that the law would be fulfilled, change how you read the commandments?

6.title: Christ and the Law
6.essay:
Every thread of this study ties off in one place. The mirror, the fence and the guide all lead, in the end, to a person. Jesus did not come to abolish the law or to ignore it. He came to keep it, to bear its curse, and to give it back to us as a gift.

Born under the law

“But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:4–5). The Lawgiver placed himself under his own law. As a baby he was circumcised and presented in the temple, and his parents “performed everything according to the Law of the Lord” (Luke 2:39). At his baptism he said, “thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15).

Think of what that meant, day after day, for some thirty years. He loved the Lord his God with all his heart and soul and mind and strength, in the carpenter’s shop and on the roads, tired, mocked and betrayed. He loved his neighbour as himself, including the neighbours who spat on him. He could ask his enemies, “Which one of you convicts me of sin?” (John 8:46), and no one could answer. He was tempted “in every respect … as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). In the garden, with the cup of wrath before him, he kept the first and greatest commandment at the greatest cost a heart has ever paid: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).

Long before, Isaiah had written, “The LORD was pleased, for his righteousness’ sake, to magnify his law and make it glorious” (Isaiah 42:21). In the life of Jesus, the law was seen at last as it was always meant to be: not a list, but a life of perfect love.

He fulfilled it

“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). To fulfil is to fill full, to bring to completion. The sacrifices were shadows, “but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17); Israel’s civil law looked for a perfectly just King; and the moral law found in him the only human life that ever matched it.

And that obedience was not only for himself. It was for us. “For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). When God looks at a believer, he sees the record of his Son: every command kept, every duty done, every day of love. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4).

He bore its curse

But the law had more to say. It did not only command; it condemned. “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them” (Galatians 3:10). That curse stood over every one of us. And here is the heart of the gospel: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). Paul quotes the law itself: “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree” (Galatians 3:13).

Stop and take that in. The only man the law could never accuse was the one man it condemned. The mirror that shows our sin was turned towards the cross, and in it the holy God saw our guilt laid on his Son. “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5). The cry “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34) was the curse of the law falling, in full, on the one who had kept it in full.

At Sinai the mountain burned and thundered, and the people “stood far off” and begged that God would not speak to them, “lest we die” (Exodus 20:18–19). At Calvary the storm of that law broke, not on us, but on him. That is why Hebrews can say to believers, “you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest” (Hebrews 12:18), but “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24).

He gives it back as a gift

And then, risen from the dead, he hands the law back to his people: not as a covenant of works, not as a curse, but from the lips of the one who bore its penalty. The same commandments sound different in his voice. “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29–30).

It is the difference between rules pinned up by a stranger and a letter from someone who loves you. And he does not leave us to keep them alone. He pours out his Spirit, who writes the law on our hearts and gives us a new desire to walk in it: “the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death” (Romans 8:2).

The three uses, gathered in him

So every use of the law leads to Jesus. As a mirror, the law shows us our sin, and nowhere is sin seen so clearly as at the cross, where it cost the Son of God his life. As a fence, it holds back evil while the King delays his coming, so that the world has time to repent. As a guide, the law shows us the life Jesus lived, so that whoever says he abides in him “ought to walk in the same way in which he walked” (1 John 2:6).

An old woman in a hospital bed asked her pastor to read the Ten Commandments to her, one by one. He hesitated; it seemed an odd choice for a dying woman. After each commandment she whispered, “I broke that one. He kept it.” When he reached the tenth, she smiled and said, “Now read me Galatians 2:20.” She had understood everything this study has tried to say.

The law is holy, and we have broken it. Christ is holy, and he kept it, every word of it, in our place. He took its curse so that we could have his record, and then he gave us his Spirit so that we could begin to love what he loves. The law-keeper became the curse-bearer, so that law-breakers could become sons and daughters who delight in their Father’s will. There is no better news in the world.

For reflection

Which part of Jesus’ obedience to the law moves you most: his ordinary days, his love for his enemies, or Gethsemane? What does it mean for you that God sees his Son’s record when he looks at you? How do the commandments sound different when you hear them in the voice of the one who bore their curse? Could you say, with the woman in the hospital bed, “I broke that one. He kept it”?
